observations.notes: About 1 in 4 people on Earth is under 15. High birth rates in Africa and South Asia keep this number significant, though it has fallen from 1 in 3 just 50 years ago.

entity.name: Children under 15
entity.description: People aged 0-14

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Children under 15 make up a much larger share of the population in Africa and South Asia than in Europe or East Asia — birth rates in sub-Saharan Africa are roughly 4–5 times higher than in Japan
In Niger, more than half the population is under 15 — one of the youngest age structures in the world, compared to under 15% in most of Europe
36.4% of Pakistan's population consists of children aged 0–14 (under 15 years old)
24% of India's population falls within the 0–14 age bracket (under 15 years old)
"India has roughly 350 million children under 15 — more than the entire population of the United States"
28% of Bangladesh's population belongs to the 0–14 age demographic (under 15 years old)

observations.notes: Around 10% of the world is over 65 — a proportion that will double by 2050 as populations in wealthy nations age rapidly.

entity.name: People over 65
entity.description: People aged 65 and over

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: The share of people over 65 is rising in almost every country — driven by falling birth rates and longer lives — creating new pressures on pension and healthcare systems
Japan leads the world in population ageing — nearly 30% of its population is over 65, compared to under 3% in many sub-Saharan African countries

observations.notes: For the first time in history, more than half of humanity lives in urban areas. By 2050 that will be closer to 700 out of 1,000.

entity.name: Urban residents
entity.description: People living in cities or urban areas

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Lagos, Dhaka, and Delhi each add millions of residents every year — cities in the global south now account for most of the world's urban population growth
In 1950 only about 30 in every 100 people lived in cities; by 2050 that figure is expected to reach 68 — urbanisation has been one of the defining shifts of the modern era
Sub-Saharan Africa is the world's fastest-urbanising region, with around 45% of its population already in cities — yet it remains less urbanised than every other major world region

observations.notes: The world has about 4 doctors per 1,000 people globally, but this hides enormous inequality — some wealthy nations have 35 per 1,000 while some low-income nations have fewer than 0.2.

entity.name: Doctors
entity.description: Registered medical doctors worldwide

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Most of the world's doctors are clustered in wealthy countries — sub-Saharan Africa has less than 3% of global physicians despite holding 16% of the world's population
The US alone has more registered doctors than all of sub-Saharan Africa combined — medical training and healthcare investment are heavily concentrated in high-income nations
Global physician numbers have grown 60% since 2000, but mostly in countries that were already well-supplied — the distribution gap has barely narrowed
Norway has about 40 doctors per 1,000 people; Niger has fewer than 0.1 — a 400-fold gap driven by wealth, training capacity, and migration of healthcare workers to richer countries

observations.notes: There are roughly 10 nurses and midwives per 1,000 people globally, forming the backbone of healthcare in most of the world.

entity.name: Nurses and midwives
entity.description: Registered nurses and midwives worldwide

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Nurses and midwives outnumber doctors roughly two to one globally, and in many rural areas they are the only healthcare providers that communities ever see
Sub-Saharan Africa faces a shortage of over 4 million nurses — its healthcare systems rely heavily on community health workers who have no formal nursing qualification

observations.notes: Roughly 70 million primary school teachers serve the world's 700 million primary-age students — an average class size of about 24, though in many regions classes have 50+ students.

entity.name: Primary school teachers
entity.description: Teachers working at primary school level

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Teacher shortages are far more severe in low-income countries than high-income ones — in many wealthy nations teacher-to-student ratios have improved for decades, while in sub-Saharan Africa they've worsened
Sub-Saharan Africa will need to hire around 17 million more teachers by 2030 just to achieve universal primary education — in some schools there is one teacher for 60 or more children

observations.notes: About 28% of the global workforce is in agriculture, mostly smallholder farmers in Asia and Africa. In wealthy nations this figure is under 5%.

entity.name: Agricultural workers
entity.description: People working in agriculture farming fishing or forestry

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: More than 90% of the world's farms are smallholdings under 2 hectares — most are in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where agriculture remains the primary livelihood for billions
The share of the workforce in agriculture is dramatically higher in low-income countries — in Ethiopia over 70% work the land, while in the UK and US it's under 2%

In South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, roughly half of all workers are in agriculture — compared to under 5% in wealthy nations, reflecting how mechanisation has transformed farming in richer countries

Over the past three decades, South Asia's agricultural workforce contracted significantly to two-thirds of its 1990 baseline. By contrast, sub-Saharan Africa experienced a much more gradual transition, with its 2023 farming workforce retaining five-sixths of its 1990 level.

observations.notes: Around 700–900 million people live on less than $2.15 per day (2017 PPP). This figure has fallen dramatically — it was over 1,900 per 1,000 in 1990.

entity.name: People in extreme poverty
entity.description: People living on under $2.15 per day

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: The share of people in extreme poverty fell from nearly 40% in 1990 to under 10% by 2019 — then stalled as COVID-19, conflict, and climate disruption reversed progress in many regions
More than 90% of people in extreme poverty live in sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia — in some countries more than half the population lives below the $2.15-a-day line
In the Democratic Republic of Congo, over 75% of the population lives in extreme poverty — one of the highest rates anywhere in the world

observations.notes: About two-thirds of humanity is now online. The remaining third — mostly in rural sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — are the focus of major connectivity efforts.

entity.name: Internet users
entity.description: People with access to the internet

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: India crossed 800 million internet users in 2023 — a single country now has more people online than the entire world did in 2005, reflecting how fast connectivity has spread

Internet access has grown faster than almost any technology in history — from fewer than 1 in 50 people in 1997 to a clear majority today — yet hundreds of millions remain offline, mostly in rural Africa and South Asia
Sub-Saharan Africa has the lowest internet penetration of any world region — around 40% of people were online in 2023, compared to over 90% in Europe and North America

observations.notes: About one-third of humanity is still offline. These people, mostly in rural sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — are the focus of major connectivity efforts.

entity.name: People without internet access
entity.description: People with no access to the internet

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: While Europe/North america has 90% internet availability, only 40% in sub-Saharan africa have access
"Ethiopia: 106.7 million people offline. This represents one of the lowest percentages of connectivity globally, with over 75% of the population cut off."
By 2023, India had more internet users than the number of internet users in the entire world back in 2005. In other words, internet penetration has been dramatic in the last 2 decades.

observations.notes: More than half of all people now carry a smartphone — a technology that barely existed 20 years ago. Mobile phones have leapfrogged wired infrastructure in the developing world.

entity.name: Smartphone owners
entity.description: People who own a smartphone

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: China and India together account for roughly a third of all smartphone users on Earth — scale in just two countries that dwarfs most continents
More people now own a smartphone than have access to safely managed drinking water — consumer technology has spread faster than basic infrastructure in many regions
In sub-Saharan Africa, smartphone ownership has grown rapidly but still lags behind other regions — around 40–50% of adults owned a smartphone in 2023, compared to over 80% in Europe

observations.notes: Global adult literacy stands at around 87%. The 13% who cannot read are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and among women in conservative regions.

entity.name: Literate adults
entity.description: Adults who can read and write

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: About two-thirds of the world's illiterate adults are women — and most are concentrated in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, where gender gaps in schooling remain wide
Global adult literacy has risen dramatically since 1970, driven by the expansion of schooling in Asia and Latin America — but progress has been slower in parts of sub-Saharan Africa
In Mali, around 35% of adults can read and write — among the lowest literacy rates globally — while in wealthy countries near-universal literacy has been achieved for generations

observations.notes: The world produces enough food — about 2,850 calories per person per day — to feed everyone. Hunger persists due to distribution failures, poverty, and waste, not global scarcity.

entity.name: Daily food calories available
entity.description: Calories available per person per day from food supply

metric.name: Per-capita daily rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per day

facts.text: The world produces enough calories to feed every person — the challenge is that food is unevenly distributed, with wealthy populations consuming far more than they need while hundreds of millions go hungry
The United States throws away enough food each year to provide every American with 1,400 calories a day — while 700 million people globally go to bed hungry

observations.notes: About 1.3 billion tonnes of food — roughly one-third of all food produced — is wasted each year. In wealthy nations most waste is at the consumer end; in poor nations it's mostly post-harvest losses.

entity.name: Annual food wasted
entity.description: Food lost or wasted globally per year

metric.name: Annual total flow
metric.description: Total quantity produced or lost per year globally

facts.text: In high-income countries, most food is wasted at the retail and consumer stage; in low-income countries, losses happen mostly at harvest, storage, and transport — very different problems with very different solutions
Food waste has barely declined in wealthy nations despite decades of awareness campaigns — reducing it remains one of the cheapest ways to cut agricultural emissions
North Americans and Europeans waste roughly 95–115 kg of food per person per year, compared to just 6–11 kg per person in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia

observations.notes: The global average is about 185 liters per person per day across all uses (drinking, cooking, sanitation, agriculture). Americans use ~500 liters; many Africans survive on under 20 liters.

entity.name: Daily freshwater consumption
entity.description: Freshwater used per person per day across all uses

metric.name: Per-capita daily rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per day

facts.text: Agriculture accounts for about 70% of all freshwater withdrawals globally — meaning the water footprint of food production dwarfs household consumption

Water use is heavily skewed by wealth and geography — a typical resident of a high-income country uses far more water indirectly through food and goods than someone in a low-income country uses in total
Americans use roughly 500 litres of water per day; people in Mozambique or Niger typically use under 20 litres — a 25-fold gap that reflects both water scarcity and lack of infrastructure

observations.notes: About 2.2 billion people lack access to safely managed drinking water. This is one of the most preventable causes of death and disease worldwide.

entity.name: People without safe drinking water
entity.description: People lacking safely managed drinking water

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Most people without safe water live in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — and the burden falls disproportionately on women and girls, who often walk hours daily to collect it

Access to safe water varies enormously even within countries — urban residents in most parts of the world have tap water, while many rural communities in Africa and Asia rely on unprotected wells or rivers
In Ethiopia, around 40% of the population lacks access to basic drinking water — one of the higher rates in the world, concentrated in rural and remote areas

observations.notes: The average person uses about 3,300 kWh of electricity per year. Americans use ~12,000 kWh; the global average hides vast inequality — an American uses 10× more than someone in Ethiopia.

entity.name: Annual electricity consumed
entity.description: Electricity consumed per person per year

metric.name: Per-capita annual rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per year

facts.text: An average American uses about 10 times more electricity per year than the global average — electricity consumption tracks wealth more closely than almost any other resource
Global electricity demand has more than doubled since 1990, driven by population growth, industrialisation in Asia, and the rise of consumer electronics
Sub-Saharan Africa generates about 1% of global electricity despite holding roughly 15% of the world's population — a stark illustration of how unequally energy is distributed

observations.notes: About 30% of global electricity now comes from renewable sources (hydro, wind, solar, etc.). This share is rising rapidly — wind and solar alone exceeded 13% in 2023.

entity.name: Renewable electricity share
entity.description: Share of electricity generated from renewable sources

metric.name: Percentage share
metric.description: Fraction of a whole expressed per 1000 units

facts.text: The share of renewables in global electricity has roughly doubled since 2010, driven mostly by the dramatic fall in wind and solar costs — both now cheaper than new coal in most markets
Solar energy is growing faster than any fuel in history — capacity added globally in 2023 exceeded all previous records, but fossil fuels still dominate total electricity generation
China installed more solar capacity in 2023 than the entire world had installed in all previous years combined — a single country driving much of the global renewable energy transition

observations.notes: About 730 million people — mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and developing Asia — still have no access to electricity. This number has fallen from 1.2 billion in 2010.

entity.name: People without electricity access
entity.description: People lacking any access to electricity

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: People without electricity are overwhelmingly concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — and for many, cooking with solid fuels causes more immediate harm than lack of light
The number of people without electricity has fallen significantly since 2010, driven mainly by India's rural electrification push — but progress in sub-Saharan Africa has been much slower
Electrification rate across the Sub-Saharan region has roughly doubled since 2000
In sub-Saharan Africa, 80% of the Urban population has electricity, but over 60% of the rural population doesn't
In Chad, fewer than 10% of the population has electricity access — one of the lowest rates in the world, with most rural communities entirely off-grid
Approximately 47% to 53% of the population in Sub-Saharan Africa lives without electricity
Approximately 22% of the people in DRC Africa have access to electricity

observations.notes: An estimated 1.6 billion people live in inadequate housing — slums, informal settlements, or without any shelter. This includes 100 million who are literally homeless.

entity.name: People in inadequate housing
entity.description: People living in slums informal settlements or without shelter

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: In some sub-Saharan African cities, more than 60% of urban residents live in informal settlements or slums — far higher than in wealthier regions where slums are a much smaller fraction of city populations
Inadequate housing is heavily concentrated in low-income countries — rapid urban growth has outpaced housing construction in cities across Africa, South Asia, and Latin America
Roughly 53% of India's homeless population lives in urban cities, driven by work migration and lack of affordable housing.
"There are as many  homeless/inadequate housing in Africa as in Asia + South America combined."
There are as many homeless in N. America as in Europe, but both continents have far fewer homelessness compared to the other 3 continents.

In Nigeria alone, an estimated 40–50 million people live in substandard housing or informal settlements — a single country that illustrates how large the housing deficit is in rapidly urbanising Africa
India has an official houseless population of 1.77 million people, though civil rights groups estimate the actual number is closer to 3 million.
Slum Populations: Alongside street homelessness, an estimated 65 million people reside in precarious urban slums
"Nigeria records the largest homeless and displaced population at roughly 24.4 million, followed by Egypt with about 12 million"

Global homelessness has worsened since 2000 — the number of people without adequate shelter has grown substantially, driven by rapid urbanisation outpacing housing construction, conflict displacement, and climate-related housing loss.

observations.notes: There are roughly 1.45 billion cars on Earth — about 1 for every 5 people. But car ownership is extremely unequal: the US has ~800 cars per 1,000 people; India has about 30.

entity.name: Passenger cars
entity.description: Registered passenger cars worldwide

metric.name: Object count
metric.description: Count of non-person objects (vehicles

facts.text: Car ownership rates differ enormously by wealth — the US has about 800 cars per 1,000 people; India has about 30 — a gap that reflects not just wealth but also the quality of public transport infrastructure
The wealthiest 10% of countries account for roughly 70% of all cars on the road — car ownership remains heavily concentrated in North America, Europe, and parts of East Asia
The United States alone has more than 280 million registered passenger cars — roughly one car per adult, and more than any other country by a wide margin

observations.notes: About 1.5 billion people took at least one commercial flight in 2023 (IATA). That's 150 out of every 1,000 people on Earth who fly at least once per year — flying remains a minority activity, heavily concentrated in wealthy countries.

entity.name: Annual air travelers
entity.description: People who take at least one commercial flight per year

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: Flying remains one of the most unequally distributed activities on Earth — the majority of flights are taken by a small minority of frequent flyers, mostly in wealthy countries
Most people in low-income countries have never flown — air travel is overwhelmingly the activity of wealthier populations, and the gap between rich and poor countries is enormous
The US alone accounts for roughly a quarter of all commercial passengers globally — more than all of Africa, South America, and the Middle East combined

observations.notes: The global average GDP per capita is about $13,500/year, but the median person earns far less. The US average is ~$65,000; the average in low-income countries is under $1,000.

entity.name: GDP per capita
entity.description: Gross domestic product per person at purchasing power parity

metric.name: Per-capita annual rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per year

facts.text: The average person in the world's 10 richest countries earns roughly 50 times more than the average person in the 10 poorest — a gap that has barely narrowed in decades
The global average income is pulled up dramatically by a small number of very wealthy countries — the typical person on Earth earns far less than the average suggests
Luxembourg's GDP per capita exceeds $120,000 per year; Burundi's is under $300 — a 400-fold gap that illustrates how little the global average tells you about any individual country

observations.notes: The wealthiest 10% of people hold about 76% of all global wealth. The bottom 50% hold less than 2%. Wealth inequality is far more extreme than income inequality.

entity.name: Top 10% wealth share
entity.description: Share of all global wealth held by the wealthiest 10%

metric.name: Percentage share
metric.description: Fraction of a whole expressed per 1000 units

facts.text: Wealth inequality is far more extreme than income inequality — owning assets (property, shares) compounds advantage over time in a way that wages alone do not
Wealth inequality worsened after the 2008 financial crisis as stock and property prices recovered faster than wages, benefiting those who already owned assets
North America and Europe together hold more than 60% of all global household wealth, despite containing less than 20% of the world's population

observations.notes: The world loses about 47 million hectares of forest each year — an area the size of Sweden — though reforestation efforts offset some of this.

entity.name: Annual forest area lost
entity.description: Forest area permanently lost per year due to deforestation

metric.name: Annual total flow
metric.description: Total quantity produced or lost per year globally

facts.text: Deforestation is almost entirely driven by agriculture — clearing land for cattle, soy, palm oil, and subsistence farming, not logging for timber

Brazil's Amazon deforestation fell by roughly 80% between 2004 and 2012 under strong enforcement policies — then rebounded sharply when those policies weakened, showing deforestation is a political choice
Brazil, Indonesia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo together account for more than half of all tropical deforestation — three countries defining the pace of global forest loss

observations.notes: The average person emits about 4.6 tonnes of CO₂ per year. Americans emit ~14 tonnes; people in the poorest countries emit under 0.5 tonnes — a 30× gap.

entity.name: CO2 emissions per capita
entity.description: Carbon dioxide emitted per person per year from all sources

metric.name: Per-capita annual rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per year

facts.text: The richest 10% of people are responsible for about half of all global carbon emissions, while the poorest 50% produce less than 10% — climate change is overwhelmingly driven by wealthy consumption
Americans emit roughly 3 times the global average per person; people in low-income countries emit a tiny fraction of that — the gap in emissions per person between rich and poor nations is enormous
A return economy-class flight from London to New York emits roughly 1 tonne of CO₂ per passenger — about as much as an average person in Rwanda emits in an entire year

observations.notes: The global average life expectancy is 73 years — up from 48 in 1950. Japan leads at 84; some low-income nations are still under 60.

entity.name: Life expectancy at birth
entity.description: Average number of years a newborn is expected to live

metric.name: Per-capita annual rate
metric.description: Quantity consumed or available per person per year

facts.text: Life expectancy has risen dramatically since 1950, driven mainly by reductions in child mortality — but the gap between the richest and poorest countries remains more than 20 years
Japan leads global life expectancy at around 84 years; Chad sits at around 54 years — a 30-year gap driven by differences in healthcare, nutrition, water access, and conflict

Sub-Saharan Africa has an average life expectancy of around 62 years — more than 10 years below the global average, with the gap driven largely by preventable diseases and limited healthcare infrastructure

observations.notes: About 260 million children and youth are out of school. Most are in conflict-affected zones or the most remote rural areas of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

entity.name: Out-of-school children
entity.description: Children and youth not enrolled in primary or secondary school

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: More than half of out-of-school children live in conflict-affected countries — places where schools have been destroyed, teachers have fled, and families are displaced
Out-of-school rates are far higher for girls than boys in many parts of sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia — gender, poverty, and conflict compound one another to keep children out of education

In Nigeria alone, there are an estimated 20 million out-of-school children — the highest number of any country in the world, driven by poverty, insecurity in the north, and the collapse of schools in conflict zones

observations.notes: Over 114 million people are forcibly displaced — including 36 million refugees who have fled their home countries — the highest figure ever recorded.

entity.name: Forcibly displaced people
entity.description: People displaced by conflict persecution or disaster

metric.name: Population count
metric.description: Count of people with a given characteristic

facts.text: The number of forcibly displaced people has more than doubled since 2012, driven by prolonged conflicts that show no sign of resolution — displacement is increasingly long-term, not temporary

Most refugees are hosted not by wealthy countries but by neighbouring low-income nations — countries like Uganda, Iran, and Colombia host millions despite having far fewer resources than European or North American states
Sudan's conflict alone has produced over 8 million internally displaced people since 2023 — a single crisis straining the entire global humanitarian system
